Progression-free survival (PFS) Add-on radical local therapy possibly improved PFS by 40% (HR: 0.60, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.80; 9 RCTs with 685 participants; low certainty of evidence) ( figure 2B ). Between-trial heterogeneity led to a median of 43% variation in the HR (median HR: 1.43), which is slightly more than the estimated 40% reduction in the hazard explained by the intervention (ie, add-on radical local therapy). We found evidence for non-proportionality of hazards in several trials ( online supplemental appendix ), further necessitating RMSTD calculation. It led to longer progression-free survival by 1.83 months (0.98 to 2.68) over 1 year. It led to increase by 3.43 months (1.22 to 5.65) over 2 years and by 4.08 months (0.28 to 7.87) over 3 years ( figure 3B ). The funnel plot is fairly symmetrical (Egger’s regression: p=0.29) ( online supplemental appendix ). Safety Most of the studies have concluded that radical local therapy is well tolerated with few serious adverse events. 9 47 48 Skin rash, pruritus, nausea and pneumonitis occurrences are most common adverse events. 8 9 There was no significant difference between radical local therapy and systemic therapy groups in safety terms. 8 Few studies like Shan et al found more haemoptysis and pneumothorax with radical local therapy. 8 16 49 Gomez et al reported more number of death with systemic therapy. 47 Lim et al found more progression to brain metastasis with systemic therapy. 46 Sensitivity analysis We conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding three studies, two which included patients with oligoprogression, 16 52 and another that only included patients with CNS metastases. 46 The results remained consistent with the estimate for OS changing from HR 0.62 (0.50 to 0.76) to HR 0.47 (0.36 to 0.61). RMSTD for OS at a follow-up period of 4 years changed from 6.65 months (4.05 to 9.24) to 9.79 months (6.53 to 13.06). Similarly, PFS changed from HR 0.60 (0.45 to 0.80) to 0.54 (0.41 to 0.72). The RMSTD for PFS at a follow-up period of 3 years changed from 4.08 months (0.28 to 7.87) to 4.98 months (1.51 to 8.44). In the primary analysis, RMSTD for OS at a follow-up period of 4 years was estimated at 6.65 months (4.05 to 9.24). The result remained consistent in sensitivity analyses for different methods of pooling the results, ranging from 6.66 months (3.72 to 9.6) to 7.66 months (2.81 to 12.51). The results remained consistent for all the assessed timepoints for both OS and PFS ( online supplemental appendix ). A conventional meta-analysis using reported HR showed similar estimates with OS changing from HR 0.62 (0.50 to 0.76) to HR 0.63 (0.42 to 0.93), and PFS changing from HR 0.60 (0.45 to 0.80) to 0.51 (0.33 to 0.79). RMSTD could not be computed for the conventional meta-analysis. Subgroup analysis could not be performed based on intervention type because of diverse intervention subtypes with one study assessing surgery or radiotherapy as required, and other studies assessing varying doses and regimens of radiotherapy. 8 48 49 Most of the studies did not furnish data adequately for the different subgroups for our use case. And exploratory analyses were either not done or not reliable due to a smaller number of participants in different categories. This limited our ability to conduct subgroup analysis. However, since some studies did report exploratory analyses, and some used dynamic or stratified randomisation based on other prognostic variables, 9 16 47 we have narratively summarised the results of exploratory analyses from these studies in table 1 . Discussion We found that add-on radical local therapy improved OS by 38% compared with systemic therapy alone in oligometastatic NSCLC. It led to longer OS by a half of a month over 1 year, increasing to 6.65 months over 4 years. It also possibly improved PFS by 40% and led to longer PFS by 1.83 months over 1 year, increasing to 4.08 months over 3 years. There was no major difference in serious adverse events between the two groups. Radical local therapy for oligometastatic lung cancer commonly involves two modalities, surgery and radiotherapy. However, most studies have used radiotherapy which has historically served as a palliative modality in metastatic NSCLC through diverse immunologic effects in modulation of the tumour microenvironment. 53 Radiotherapy is great option for the treatment of oligometastatic disease as it is a non-invasive method delivering ablative doses of external beam radiotherapy to the target tumour while minimising dose to the surrounding normal tissues. 54 In patients with oligometastatic NSCLC, ionising radiation also acts by producing greater antigen presentation for better immune system recognition. 55 Radical local therapy acts by dual action through increasing the sensitivity of the tumour cells to chemotherapy and arresting the spread of distant metastases. 56 Radical local therapy is preferable at the time of progression rather than early on, as it may also inhibit the metastasised tumour burden. In previous systematic reviews, assessing add-on radical local therapy in oligometastatic NSCLC, OS and PFS has been reported separately for both radical local therapy and systemic therapy. 14 15 However, they were not compared between the interventions. And subtracting the estimates in both groups does not provide the exact difference. Moreover, this does not yield the CI, and hence, we cannot judge the precision of difference. We have instead provided the restricted difference in both OS and PFS at several timepoints. Some systematic reviews did compare the two groups directly. However, they have included both RCTs and retrospective studies. 13 15 Li et al found no difference, reporting an imprecise HR of 1.61 (95% CI 0.86 to 3.03). 57 In contrast, Petrelli et al observed 56% and 58% reduction in the hazards for OS and PFS. 58 Our study aligns with Petrelli et al , showing an improvement in both OS and PFS (38% and 40% respectively). The variation in results compared with previous studies could be explained by the inclusion of both retrospective studies and RCTs. It is reported that RCTs can better assess the survival among cancer patients. 59 This previous systematic review included two RCTs. 58 Our study, which includes the most recent and maximum number (10) of RCTs, likely reflects this improved credibility of results. Most of the studies have expressed PFS and OS as HR and, as discussed earlier, the PH assumption does not always hold true. 14 58 60 61 This was also highlighted in our study as this assumption was violated in at least one trial included to assess OS, and multiple trials included to assess PFS. Thus, HR may not be the appropriate measure to assess intervention effect here, and we decided to use RMSTD instead. We could assess the survival time benefit (as RMSTD) for OS up to 4 years, and for PFS up to 3 years. The reason is that we prioritised robustness of analysis over misleading data. In the data for PFS, the survival curve shows that only 5% of the initial participants were progression-free at the end of 3 years, and hence, very limited patients contributed additional data for the fourth year. This contrasts with 34% and 17% of the participants (in the experimental and control arms, respectively) surviving by 3 years, and thereby providing additional data for OS at 4 years. Therefore, since the statistical model assumptions were not met for RMSTD of PFS at 4 years, we did not compute this data. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for OS and PFS in oligometastatic NSCLC is not available in the published literature. The only related studies discussed MCID for outcomes like quality of life. 62 , 65 Nevertheless, even minor improvements in critical direct outcomes like survival/mortality are considered important. Hence, an effect of this magnitude—increase in 6 months of overall survival over 4 years, and an increase in 4 months of progression-free survival over 3 years—can be considered to be clinically important. Most meta-analyses have reported adverse events narratively, as the available data from individual studies are incompatible for pooling, making it difficult to reach a more definitive conclusion. 66 67 Previous reviews have shown that radical local therapy is well tolerated. 68 Similarly, in our study, adverse events were largely comparable between radical local therapy and standard care, and radical local therapy is well tolerated among most of the patients. However, chemotherapy is linked to a higher rate of tumour progression at the original site and distant spread, due to which patients were switched to radical local therapy group. 47 48 This further reinforces our findings, highlighting a more favourable risk-benefit ratio for the radical local therapy group. Radical local therapy has shown promising role in other oligometastatic cancers too. In prostate cancer, the role of radical local therapy was earlier only in palliative care, but recent studies demonstrate its role in oligometastatic cancer patients. Progression-free survival is also found to be increased significantly with radiotherapy. 69 In oligometastatic liver cancer, SBRT has shown an increased local control rate of up to 96%, though there is no definitive evidence on overall survival. 70 Our study includes 10 RCTs, much than any other meta-analysis (MA), and did not combine RCTs with retrospective studies. Studies have shown that RMSTD is more robust, clinically interpretable and typically yields more conservative estimates than those derived from HRs, making it a more reliable basis for conclusions. 21 There are IPD meta-analyses on various aspects of chemotherapy in NSCLC. 71 , 73 However, no IPD meta-analyses are currently available to explore the role of add-on radical local therapy in oligometastatic NSCLC. A limitation is that we could not retrieve data on covariates. We had contacted the trial investigators but could not obtain this information. Subgroup analyses could not be performed, but nevertheless, the low median HR shows that between-study heterogeneity was not an issue and the results were favourable regardless. We did not assess OS and PFS at 5 years because statistical assumptions were not met due to less evidence at these timepoints. Hence, we preferred to avoid misestimation and reported until the 3–4-year timepoint where the statistical model assumptions were met. Further, some advantages of IPD like including covariates could not be incorporated because we could not obtain the data from the trial investigators. Nevertheless, other advantages, like more precise and interpretable estimates, were obtained. We complemented the IPD approach with a standard MA on reported HR. Formal tests for publication bias could not be conducted, but we did not find any evidence of reporting bias. Although radical local therapy showed significant change in overall and progression-free survival, most of the studies are about radiotherapy even though radiotherapy was introduced later in local therapy. Surgery remains an area for further exploration in oligometastatic NSCLC studies, as there is limited evidence supporting its role in radical local therapy, with most evidence coming from early stage NSCLC. 74 75 Additionally, studies have indicated that patients in the programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) negative group benefit more from radical local therapy, suggesting that future RCTs should focus on PD-L1 status to further investigate this potential covariate, opening the scope for personalised therapy. Moreover, complete results from ongoing studies may further improve the certainty in the evidence. 76 This systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis shows add-on radical local therapy—chiefly radiotherapy with ablative techniques—improves overall survival and possibly improves progression-free survival compared with systemic therapy alone, without major safety concerns. Future studies may address the treatment outcomes of these local therapies in combination with PD-L1 expression-based therapies. Future research could investigate the role of surgery as a form of radical local therapy and compare it with radiotherapy to provide clearer evidence for selecting the most appropriate radical local therapy. documents.title: Once- or twice-daily thoracic radiation in limited-stage small-cell lung cancer treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy.
documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To evaluate the benefits and harms of once-daily radiotherapy versus twice-daily radiotherapy concurrently with chemotherapy for optimal survival outcomes in people with limited-stage small-cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC).

The objectives are as follows: To evaluate the benefits and harms of once‐daily radiotherapy versus twice‐daily radiotherapy concurrently with chemotherapy for optimal survival outcomes in people with limited‐stage small‐cell lung cancer (LS‐SCLC). pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC New Background Description of the condition Lung cancer is now the most frequent form of cancer and the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, accounting for an estimated 2.5 million new cases annually and 12.4% of all incident cancer cases, according to Global Cancer Statistics 2022 [ 1 ]. Of those, small‐cell lung cancer (SCLC) comprises nearly 15%. Rapid proliferation is a defining characteristic of SCLC. Frequent mediastinal involvement, early distant metastases, and high response rates to both chemotherapy and radiotherapy are observed [ 2 ]. A large central tumor often invades or compresses the mediastinum [ 3 ]. Paraneoplastic syndromes are common in SCLC [ 4 ]. The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified it as the most frequent histology among neuroendocrine tumors since the 2015 revision, with two subclasses: small‐cell carcinoma and combined small‐cell carcinoma [ 5 ]. No clear prognostic difference by histologic subtype has been reported [ 6 ]. Smoking is strongly associated with an increased risk of SCLC [ 7 ], the disease being most common in heavy smokers. The female gender has been associated with improved response and survival. Performance status is a strong and reproducible prognostic factor [ 8 , 9 , 10 ]. Fatigue is the most common symptom, with decreased physical activity, cough, dyspnea, and pain being other symptoms [ 11 ]. Paraneoplastic Cushing's syndrome has been correlated with a poor response to therapy and short survival [ 12 ]. The time between the start of chemotherapy and the end of radiotherapy is considered important for survival. This short time interval (less than 30 days) has shown a five‐year overall survival of over 20% [ 13 ]. Approximately 30% of people with SCLC present with localized tumors [ 2 ]. Screening computed tomography did not detect SCLC at earlier stages in several screening studies [ 14 , 15 , 16 ]. Two categorical definitions of limited‐stage (LS) or extensive‐stage (ES) SCLC have been used universally to decide treatment strategy besides the Tumour, Node, and Metastases (TNM) classification [ 17 ]. Overall, LS‐SCLC is a disease confined to one hemithorax, the contralateral mediastinum, and contralateral supraclavicular lymph nodes that can be safely encompassed within a radiation field without malignant pleural or pericardial effusions. In applying the TNM classifications to the original Veterans Administration Lung Study Group category (LS and ES definition), LS‐SCLC is defined as stage I to III (T1 to 4, N0 to 3, M0 according to the eighth lung TNM classification) [ 18 ]. Bulky primaries with multiple metastatic nodes are considered to increase the risk of chemoradiation toxicities and so should be excluded. The International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer has confirmed the prognostic value of both clinical and pathologic TNM staging in individuals with LS‐SCLC [ 19 ]. Consequently, prospective clinical trials will begin to include the TNM method because it will allow for more precise assessments of prognosis and specific therapy in the future. Clinical outcomes based on TNM staging of a phase III study in a subgroup analysis for LS‐SCLC have already been reported [ 20 ]. Description of the intervention and how it might work Current standard of care Currently, the standard of care for LS‐SCLC is twice‐daily radiotherapy concurrent with chemotherapy (four cycles of cisplatin + etoposide) [ 21 ]. Compared to chemotherapy alone, treatment‐related deaths only increased by 1.2% [ 22 , 23 ]. Prophylactic cranial irradiation would be considered if a complete remission is obtained after chemotherapy with radiotherapy [ 24 ]. Sequential treatments are considered for older adults or when performance status is poor. Radiotherapy would be delivered if tumor reduction, performance status improvement, or diminished pleural effusion is observed after chemotherapy. Radiotherapy is not offered to people with apparent interstitial lung disease. In many countries, once‐daily radiotherapy is still prevalent [ 25 , 26 , 27 ], because twice‐daily radiotherapy has logistical issues and inconveniences for people with no statistical difference in survival between the two regimens. A higher frequency of grade 3 esophagitis has been observed with twice‐daily radiotherapy [ 28 ], but overall, long‐term toxicities are not different between the two regimens ( Table 1 ). The twice‐daily radiotherapy evidence was first published in 1999 [ 28 ]. Then, modern and precise radiation techniques such as intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), and image‐guided radiotherapy (IGRT) have largely supplanted older conventional radiotherapy. IMRT and VMAT can spare more unaffected organs by developing a concave radiotherapy area around critical organs at risk. Postchemotherapy tumor volume and involved‐field radiotherapy (IFRT) are now applied to reduce toxicities. In recent years, at least two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated the efficacy of twice‐daily and once‐daily radiation schedules [ 29 , 30 ]. In these two studies, median overall survival ranged from 28.7 to 30 months in the twice‐daily group and 25 to 30.5 months in the once‐daily group. Even after those trials, optimal radiation regimens remain uncertain for LS‐SCLC. For this reason, we would like to contribute to investigating optimal radiation regimens for people with LS‐SCLC. 1 Summary of esophagus, lung and cardiac toxicity Esophagitis Pneumonitis Cardiac Frequency 2% [ 64 ] – 32% [ 28 ] (twice‐daily) 5% [ 65 ] – 19% [ 29 ] (once‐daily) (≥ grade 3) 10% or lower [ 29 , 66 , 67 ] (≥ grade 3) 0.01% [ 29 ] (death) – 0.7% [ 68 ] (severe or lethal) Risk factors Dose limits Volume of esophagus receiving ≥ 15 Gy [ 69 ] (twice‐daily) Volume of esophagus receiving ≥ 60 Gy [ 70 ] (once‐daily) V20 should be < 25% to 30% [ 71 , 72 ] (twice‐daily) V20 should be < 30% to 35% [ 73 ] (once‐daily) Limited data for LS‐SCLC Mean heart dose [ 74 ] Dose to base of heart [ 75 ] Time point Around 2 weeks after the start of radiotherapy Around 2 – 3 months after the completion of radiotherapy Cardiac deaths as a proportion of all deaths were highest after 5 years [ 68 ]. LS‐SCLC: limited‐stage small‐cell lung cancer; V20: Volume of lung receiving 20 Gy Timing of chemotherapy and radiotherapy Concurrent use of radiotherapy with cisplatin plus etoposide is recommended for LS‐SCLC [ 21 ]. In the JCOG 9104 trial, which compared concurrent versus sequential radiotherapy, the concurrent group showed a trend toward longer overall survival (median 27.2 versus 19.7 months, P = 0.097) and acceptable toxicity [ 21 ]. From this result, concurrent chemotherapy with radiotherapy is recommended over sequential treatment. In addition, several meta‐analyses on the timing of concurrent radiotherapy suggest that early radiotherapy or shorter irradiation periods (cut‐off: 30 days) improve prognosis [ 13 , 31 , 32 ]. Specifically, a systematic review found an increase in two‐year survival (risk ratio (RR) 1.17, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.35) in the early radiotherapy group (less than nine weeks from the start of chemotherapy) compared with the late radiotherapy group [ 31 ]. Another meta‐analysis revealed a greater five‐year survival rate (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.80) in the group with a shorter time between the start of chemotherapy and the end of radiotherapy [ 13 ]. Furthermore, greater two‐year (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.94) and five‐year survival rates (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.93) in the early radiotherapy group with chemotherapy have been reported [ 32 ]. All of these suggest that definitive thoracic radiotherapy should ideally be started early in the course of chemotherapy. Optimal radiotherapy dose and fractionation for LS‐SCLC Twice‐daily radiotherapy is an evidence‐based therapy for LS‐SCLC [ 21 , 28 , 29 ]. Specifically, 1.5 gray (Gy) × 30 fraction (fr) twice‐daily of 45 Gy is the standard method. This is based on the outcome of the phase III study [ 28 ], which compared once‐daily radiotherapy 45 Gy/25 fr/35 days with twice‐daily 45 Gy/30 fr/19 days. The five‐year survival rates were better in the twice‐daily group, though grade 3 esophagitis was observed more markedly in the twice‐daily group than in the conventional once‐daily group [ 28 ]. In contrast, another study found no difference in overall survival between traditional once‐daily 50.4 Gy/28 fr/38 days compared with twice‐daily 48 Gy/32 fr/20 days plus an 18‐day rest period [ 33 ]. This negative study could be attributable to the longer treatment duration owing to the rest period. Thus, twice‐daily radiotherapy is still considered standard therapy. Some researchers assert that in the Turrisi study [ 28 ], in which twice‐daily radiotherapy had a better outcome than once‐daily radiotherapy, the study outcome may have been affected by the low dose of 45 Gy in the once‐daily group, which is lower than the 60 Gy usually administered. This view and advances in radiation technologies have led to the CONVERT trial [ 29 ], which attempted to verify the superiority of a higher dose of once‐daily 66 Gy/33 fr/45 days over twice‐daily 45 Gy/30 fr/19 days. Nevertheless, the primary endpoint of overall survival was not prolonged, and no difference in progression‐free survival (PFS) and local control rate was found. Concerning adverse events, grade 4 neutropenia was more frequent in the twice‐daily group, but no difference was found in other adverse events [ 29 ]. Radiation field: the National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines Historically, after the INT0096 study, clinically uninvolved mediastinal nodes have been included in the radiotherapy target volume, whereas contralateral hilum and uninvolved supraclavicular nodes have not generally been included. The need for extended nodal irradiation (ENI) remains controversial. A phase II study found that the omission of ENI resulted in a relatively high rate of isolated nodal recurrences of 11% [ 13 ]. Nevertheless, when incorporating 18 F‐fluorodeoxyglucose‐positron emission tomography (FDG‐PET) staging, the recurrence rate was low at 3% [ 34 ]. Recent phase III prospective trials have omitted ENI (CALGB 30610/RTOG 0538; CONVERT trial) [ 29 , 30 ]. Clinical practice guidelines recommend IFRT (smaller radiotherapy field) for reduced toxicities and comparable benefits [ 35 ]. Target volumes are based on all postchemotherapy volumes at treatment planning and lymph node areas at initial diagnosis [ 35 , 36 ]. Although the magnitude of the difference in survival between twice‐daily and once‐daily radiotherapy is minimal in several prospective trials, twice‐daily radiotherapy requires multiple visits to the hospital with six‐hour intervals in the morning and afternoon. This is inconvenient for individuals and a logistically heavy workload for hospitals. In contrast, once‐daily radiotherapy can offer convenient treatment accessibility. In addition, with hypofractionated (radiotherapy > 2 Gy/fr) once‐daily radiotherapy, the overall treatment duration can be shorter than with conventionally fractionated once‐daily radiotherapy. This shorter total radiotherapy duration can be a benefit to people with LS‐SCLC. Thus, this review aims to determine whether the once‐daily radiotherapy regimen, which is more convenient for individuals and practical for treatment centers, can provide equivalent outcomes to the twice‐daily radiotherapy regimen. To achieve this, we will conduct a systematic review and meta‐analysis that includes recent phase III prospective trials. Why it is important to do this review There are discrepancies in adopting twice‐daily radiotherapy worldwide [ 25 , 26 , 27 ]. Although the recommended strategy is twice‐daily radiotherapy for LS‐SCLC, several factors could affect whether to use twice‐daily or once‐daily radiotherapy for individuals with LS‐SCLC. For example, these include the participant's age, accessibility to the hospital, financial and physical burdens of transportation, and family support for hospital visits. We have found no Cochrane review on twice‐daily or once‐daily radiotherapy for LS‐SCLC. Although there are systematic reviews similar to our study [ 37 , 38 , 39 ], these reviews are not up‐to‐date. In addition, these reviews have methodological issues such as the absence of a registered protocol and no risk of bias assessment. Moreover, these already published reviews include non‐RCTs with discordant results. Further, ongoing research results combined with immunotherapies are awaited. Therefore, we need to conduct a standard and rigorous Cochrane review to build robust evidence on this topic. Objectives To evaluate the benefits and harms of once‐daily radiotherapy versus twice‐daily radiotherapy concurrently with chemotherapy for optimal survival outcomes in people with limited‐stage small‐cell lung cancer (LS‐SCLC). Methods We will follow the Methodological Expectations for Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) when conducting the review [ 40 ], and PRISMA 2020 for the reporting [ 41 ]. Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include parallel randomized controlled trials (RCTs). We will exclude cross‐over trials, cluster‐randomized trials and quasi‐randomized trials (using a non‐random process) because they are inappropriate designs for the participants and intervention considered in this review. We will include RCTs reporting on the benefits and harms of twice‐daily and once‐daily radiotherapy for limited‐stage small‐cell lung cancer (LS‐SCLC), with or without blinding. There will be no restrictions on language or publication status. We will include meeting abstracts and unpublished online data only when sufficient data are provided. Phase II trials will be eligible as long as they are randomized correctly. We will include studies regardless of the outcomes reported. Types of participants We will include adult participants (18 years of age or older) with histologically proven localized SCLC (LS‐SCLC or TNM I‐III) treated with curative intent using concurrent cisplatin plus etoposide and definitive thoracic radiotherapy. Types of interventions We will investigate the following comparisons. Intervention: once‐daily radiotherapy with concurrent chemotherapy Control: twice‐daily radiotherapy with concurrent chemotherapy Once‐daily radiotherapy is conventional fractionation (1.8 to 2 Gy/fr) or hypofractionation (fraction size greater than 1.8 to 2 Gy/fr). Twice‐daily radiotherapy is 45 Gy over 19 days (1.5 Gy/fr, called hyperfractionation). We will apply no limitations on curative radiotherapy dose (dose escalation) or treatment duration. If a trial includes multiple arms, we will include any arm that meets the review's inclusion criteria (concurrent thoracic radiotherapy with cisplatin plus etoposide). Thoracic radiotherapy can be delivered using high‐energy X‐ray beams with linear accelerators. Radiation delivery techniques include 3‐dimensional conformal radiotherapy, intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), and volume‐modulated arc therapy (VMAT). The radiotherapy volume can involve field, volume on planning computed tomography (CT) images, or tumor volume after the first course of chemotherapy, defined using CT images with or without positron emission tomography (PET). Radiotherapy planning may include techniques to manage target motion such as, but not limited to, four‐dimensional CT simulation. Radiotherapy delivery techniques used to track target motion include, but are not limited to, respiratory management. Outcome measures We will manage the multiplicity of outcome measures by applying a hierarchy based on the frequency of use of the measures among the included studies [ 42 ]. We will only consider measures obtained with validated methods or scales [ 42 ]. We will only include data with the highest rank of the measure when a study reports the same outcome based on data acquired from multiple measures [ 42 ]. Critical outcomes Overall survival (in months): defined as time from randomization until death from any cause. If multiple measures for survival are available, we will use those closest to two and five years. We will visually inspect Kaplan‐Meier curves. Important outcomes Acute toxicity: includes radiotherapy‐induced esophagitis and pneumonitis (within radiation fields) and chemotherapy toxicity (nausea, vomiting, fatigue, neutropenia, and others) measured within 90 days of completing treatment, according to the Common Toxicity Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) [ 43 ]. We will use the worst recorded toxicity grade during the respective periods, and will measure the incidence of grade 2 (if available), grade 3, and grade 4 events. We will also check the included trials for the incidence of grade 5 adverse events. Late toxicity (dermatitis, esophagitis, pneumonitis, others): measured 90 days after completing treatment, based on CTCAE [ 43 ]. Median local progression‐free survival (LPFS)(in months): defined as time from randomization to radiological or clinical progression at the primary site, based on RECIST1.1 [ 44 ], or death. Search methods for identification of studies Electronic searches We will search the following electronic databases to collate all published RCTs, with no language limitations. The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in the Cochrane Library ( Supplementary material 1 ) MEDLINE, accessed via PubMed (1951 to date of search) ( Supplementary material 1 ) Embase, accessed via Elsevier (1947 to date of search) ( Supplementary material 1 ) We will search all databases using recognized words (MeSH) in MEDLINE and EMTREE in Embase, and free‐text words. We will perform the MEDLINE search using the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy and the precision‐maximizing version described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 45 ]. We will also search the following clinical registers of studies to include gray literature. World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (trialsearch.who.int/) Other professional and research organization websites, such as: Cancer Research UK (Cancer Research UK); European Medicines Agency (EMA); Japan's Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) (Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency); and China's National Medical Products Registration (NMDA) (National Medical Products Administration). We will contact trial authors to request further details on incomplete reports, including conference abstracts and information on any unpublished studies. We will use Zotero to identify retracted studies after publication (www.zotero.org). Zotero is linked to the Retraction Watch database (retractionwatch.com), and automatically pinpoints retracted studies or articles. The searches performed on the different databases also retrieve retraction notices, expressions of concern, or errata that were linked to their respective articles and studies. Searching other resources We will handsearch the references of eligible studies to identify additional studies for inclusion. We will also search the meeting abstracts of conferences from the following sources (from 2022 to the date of search). American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) (www.astro.org) European Society for Radiotherapy and Oncology (ESTRO) (www.estro.org) American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) (www.asco.org) European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) (www.esmo.org) World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC) (www.iaslc.org) International Lung Cancer Research Association (IASLC) (www.iaslc.org) European Society for Medical Oncology ImmunoOncology Congress (ESMO IO) (www.esmo.org) European Lung Cancer Conference (ELCC) (www.esmo.org) American Association of Cancer Research (AACR) (www.aacr.org) Data collection and analysis Selection of studies We will use Covidence to identify and remove potential duplicate reports [ 46 ]. Two review authors (KH and KI, TI, or KT) will independently screen all titles and abstracts identified by electronic searching to remove duplicates and unrelated reports. The same review authors will obtain the full texts for all relevant studies and independently check the eligibility of each study based on the eligibility criteria. We will resolve discordant evaluations through discussion to reach a consensus. We will involve a third review author (HS) when necessary to reach a consensus. We will categorize studies into four types (included, excluded, awaiting classification, and ongoing) based on our inclusion and exclusion criteria and guidance provided in the C ochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 47 ]. We will collate multiple reports of the same study so that the unit of interest in the review is each study rather than each report. We will contact the study authors for missing information that will help the reviewers determine study eligibility. Data extraction and management Two review authors (KH and KI, TI, or KT) will independently extract relevant data using a data extraction template form in Covidence [ 46 ]. These data will include the following items. Source : citation, study name if applicable, and contact data Study details : study design, location, setting (type and stage of disease), number of participating centers, sample size, study start and completion date, and study follow‐up Characteristics of participants : inclusion and exclusion criteria, number of participants, participant and tumor characteristics (age, sex, ethnicity, smoking status, WHO/Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, TNM stage) Characteristics of interventions : radiotherapy dose, dose/fr, number of fractions, volume treated, planning technique, quality assurance procedure, image guidance use, respiration motion management, and chemotherapy information Outcomes : primary and secondary outcomes with definitions and time points Results : number of participants allocated to each group, and for each outcome of interest: sample size, summary data for each group, an estimate of effect with confidence interval and P value, subgroup analyses, and whether analyses have been performed by intention‐to‐treat (ITT) or per‐protocol methods. Other : funding and possible conflicts of interests We will expand data acquisition for duplicate publications, companion documents, or multiple reports from primary studies by collecting all available data. If a single study was published in various reports, we will prioritize publications reporting the longest follow‐up associated with primary or secondary outcomes. If necessary, we will resolve any disagreements by discussion or consultation with a third author (HS, NY, or EO). Risk of bias assessment in included studies Two review authors (KH and KI, TI, or KT) will independently use version 2 of the Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB 2) for randomized trials to assess the quality and potential biases among the included studies [ 48 ], based on Chapter 8 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 49 ]. We will use the RoB Excel tool to implement RoB 2 (available from the risk of bias website: sites.google.com/site/riskofbiastool), following the guidelines in Chapter 7 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 50 ] . We are interested in the effect of assignment to intervention. We will assign our judgment to each domain of the tool as having a low risk of bias, high risk of bias, or some concern for each outcome, and we will provide reasons for our decision for each domain with a brief comment. We will summarize the risk of bias for important outcomes by considering all relevant outcomes. We will present a figure to summarize the risk of bias. When the two review authors cannot agree, we will consult a third review author (HS). Using RoB 2, we will consider the overall risk of bias and the following five domains. Bias arising from the randomization process Bias caused by deviations from intended interventions Bias caused by missing outcome data Bias in measurement of the outcome Bias in selection of the reported result We will assess the overall risk of bias for each outcome within a study by considering all domains relevant to the outcome (i.e. both study‐level entries, such as allocation sequence concealment, and outcome‐specific entries, such as blinding). We will contact study authors for any missing information required to make our judgments. If authors do not respond, we will assess the risk of bias based on the available information. Measures of treatment effect For time‐to‐event outcomes (overall survival, LPFS), we will use hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) to measure treatment outcomes. We will extract the HR from the included studies when it is available. When a study does not report the HR, we will indirectly estimate the HR using Kaplan‐Meier survival curves and the frequently used methods of Parmar and Tierney [ 51 , 52 ]. For the dichotomous outcome of adverse events, we will use risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs if possible. For dichotomous outcomes related to overall survival and LPFS at specific time points, we will use RRs to estimate survival rates with 95% CIs. For continuous outcomes, we will use mean differences (MDs) between treatment arms when the same scale is used for intervention outcomes. We will calculate standardized mean differences (SMDs) if different scales are used for the same outcome. Unit of analysis issues Participants will be the primary unit of analysis. For studies with multiple comparison groups that compare two or more intervention groups versus the same control group, we will first attempt to combine groups to create a single pairwise comparison. We will use multilevel meta‐analysis models to address within‐study correlation [ 53 ], as recommended in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 47 ]. For studies with multiple arms, we will include only the relevant arms. Dealing with missing data We will attempt to obtain missing data from study authors. We will conduct an ITT analysis if data are available; otherwise, we will conduct analyses using only the available data. We will examine for attrition (e.g. dropouts, losses to follow‐up, and withdrawals) and critically evaluate issues of missing data. We will not impute missing data. We will follow Cochrane recommendations when dealing with these issues related to data, as described in Chapter 10 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 54 ]. Reporting bias assessment We will seek to obtain study protocols to assess potential outcome reporting bias in the included studies. We will generate funnel plots to investigate reporting biases for the outcomes when the number of studies included in a single meta‐analysis is at least 10. The statistical test will be the linear regression test by Egger (we will consider P < 0.05 to be statistically significant). Asymmetry in a funnel plot may be caused by factors other than publication bias, such as study quality or the form of an intervention. Those may differ according to the size of the study (small study effects). Thus, we will follow the recommendations in Chapter 13 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 55 ]. Synthesis methods We will conduct meta‐analyses using the ITT population according to recommendations in Chapter 10 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 54 ]. We will use Review Manager (RevMan) for meta‐analyses [ 56 ]. One review author (KH) will input the data. A second review author (KI, TI, or KT) will double‐check the data for accuracy. We will use a random‐effects model since we expect there to be clinical diversity, and use the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator to estimate between‐trial variance. When there are at least three studies in the meta‐analysis and the estimate of heterogeneity is greater than zero, we will use the Hartung‐Knapp‐Sidik‐Jonkman method to calculate a confidence interval for the pooled effect estimate. In other scenarios (i.e. in pooled analyses of two studies, or where the estimate of heterogeneity is equal to zero) we will use the Wald‐type method [ 54 ]. The primary data synthesis will include all eligible studies. We will use the Synthesis Without Meta‐analysis (SWiM) guideline for synthesizing studies if meta‐analysis is impossible [ 57 ]. Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis We will first evaluate the overall characteristics of the studies to investigate clinical and methodological heterogeneity before deciding to pool data. Then, if the studies are sufficiently similar, we will perform a meta‐analysis. After pooling, we will perform subgroup analysis if there is statistical heterogeneity. We will follow Cochrane recommendations for the heterogeneity assessment [ 54 ]. We will graphically investigate heterogeneity using forest plots generated by RevMan before conducting meta‐analysis. If we detect profound statistical heterogeneity, we will investigate the source of heterogeneity. We will assess the statistical heterogeneity of treatment effects among studies for each outcome using the I 2 statistic to quantify the degree of heterogeneity [ 58 ]. I 2 indicates what proportion of the observed variability reflects real differences in effect size. It ranges from 0 to 100%. We will interpret I 2 as follows. 0% to 40%: is not important 40% to 75%: indicates moderate heterogeneity 75% to 100%: profound heterogeneity If we find profound (75% or more) heterogeneity, we will first check for calculation errors. Then, we will conduct subgroup analyses to explore possible causes for heterogeneity. With sufficient data, we will conduct subgroup analyses to assess the effect of heterogeneity on the primary outcome for the following subgroups. Gender (men versus women) ECOG Performance status before treatment (0 to 1 versus 2) Smoking history (never versus former and current smokers) Paraneoplastic syndromes before treatment (none versus present) The time between the start of chemotherapy and the end of radiotherapy (< 30 days versus ≥ 30 days) We will use RevMan to assess subgroup differences, as outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 54 ]. Equity‐related assessment We will not explore equity‐related characteristics widely because insufficient studies have assessed the effect of dose fractionation on various inequity factors. We will investigate whether gender acts as an effect modifier in our subgroup analyses. Nevertheless, we expect there will not be enough studies recording all data on the PROGRESS‐Plus characteristics (Place of residence, Race/ethnicity/culture/language, Occupation, Gender/sex, Religion, Education, Socioeconomic status, Social capital; personal characteristics associated with discrimination, features of relationships, time‐dependent relationships) [ 59 ]. When we find sufficient studies exploring additional characteristics of health equity during the analysis, we will include them post hoc, following Chapter 16 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 60 ]. Sensitivity analysis We will explore the robustness of the review by conducting sensitivity analyses when appropriate. We will conduct sensitivity analyses limited to our primary outcome to examine the influence of the following factors (when applicable) on effect sizes. Using a fixed‐effect model Excluding studies at high risk of bias Excluding phase II studies Certainty of the evidence assessment Two review authors (KH and KI, TI, or KT) will evaluate the certainty of the evidence for each outcome according to the GRADE approach (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias) [ 61 ]. We will provide a summary of findings table using GRADEpro GDT software [ 62 ]. We will use the four levels of the GRADE approach for the overall certainty of the evidence for each outcome as recommended in Chapter 14 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions [ 63 ]. The GRADE approach considers issues related not only to internal validity but also to external validity, such as the generalizability of results. Overall risk of bias will feed into one domain of the GRADE approach to assessing certainty of a body of evidence. We will describe any decisions to downgrade or upgrade the certainty of the evidence using footnotes and make comments for readers where necessary. If meta‐analysis for an outcome is impossible, we will present a narrative format in the summary of findings table. We will include the following outcomes in the summary of findings table. Overall survival (two‐year and five‐year) Acute esophageal and pulmonary radiotherapy toxicity within the radiation fields (within 90 days of completing treatment) and chemotherapy toxicity Late toxicity (dermatitis, esophagitis, pneumonitis, others), measured 90 days after completing treatment Median local progression‐free survival Consumer involvement No consumer was involved in this protocol. documents.title: Impact of low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening on lung cancer-related mortality.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death in the world, however lung cancer screening has not been implemented in most countries at a population level. A previous Cochrane Review found limited evidence for the effectiveness of lung cancer screening with chest radiography (CXR) or sputum cytology in reducing lung cancer-related mortality, however there has been increasing evidence supporting screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT).  OBJECTIVES: To determine whether screening for lung cancer using LDCT of the chest reduces lung cancer-related mortality and to evaluate the possible harms of LDCT screening.
SEARCH METHODS: We performed the search in collaboration with the Information Specialist of the Cochrane Lung Cancer Group and included the Cochrane Lung Cancer Group Trial Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, the Cochrane Library, current issue), MEDLINE (accessed via PubMed) and Embase in our search. We also searched the clinical trial registries to identify unpublished and ongoing trials. We did not impose any restriction on language of publication. The search was performed up to 31 July 2021.  SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of lung cancer screening using LDCT and reporting mortality or harm outcomes.  DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors were involved in independently assessing trials for eligibility, extraction of trial data and characteristics, and assessing risk of bias of the included trials using the Cochrane RoB 1 tool. We assessed the certainty of evidence using GRADE. Primary outcomes were lung cancer-related mortality and harms of screening. We performed a meta-analysis, where appropriate, for all outcomes using a random-effects model. We only included trials in the analysis of mortality outcomes if they had at least 5 years of follow-up. We reported risk ratios (RRs) and hazard ratios (HRs), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and used the I2 statistic to investigate heterogeneity.  MAIN RESULTS: We included 11 trials in this review with a total of 94,445 participants. Trials were conducted in Europe and the USA in people aged 40 years or older, with most trials having an entry requirement of ≥ 20 pack-year smoking history (e.g. 1 pack of cigarettes/day for 20 years or 2 packs/day for 10 years etc.). One trial included male participants only. Eight trials were phase three RCTs, with two feasibility RCTs and one pilot RCT. Seven of the included trials had no screening as a comparison, and four trials had CXR screening as a comparator. Screening frequency included annual, biennial and incrementing intervals. The duration of screening ranged from 1 year to 10 years. Mortality follow-up was from 5 years to approximately 12 years.  None of the included trials were at low risk of bias across all domains. The certainty of evidence was moderate to low across different outcomes, as assessed by GRADE. In the meta-analysis of trials assessing lung cancer-related mortality, we included eight trials (91,122 participants), and there was a reduction in mortality of 21% with LDCT screening compared to control groups of no screening or CXR screening (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.87; 8 trials, 91,122 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). There were probably no differences in subgroups for analyses by control type, sex, geographical region, and nodule management algorithm. Females appeared to have a larger lung cancer-related mortality benefit compared to males with LDCT screening. There was also a reduction in all-cause mortality (including lung cancer-related) of 5% (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.99; 8 trials, 91,107 participants; moderate-certainty evidence).  Invasive tests occurred more frequently in the LDCT group (RR 2.60, 95% CI 2.41 to 2.80; 3 trials, 60,003 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, analysis of 60-day postoperative mortality was not significant between groups (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.94; 2 trials, 409 participants; moderate-certainty evidence).  False-positive results and recall rates were higher with LDCT screening compared to screening with CXR, however there was low-certainty evidence in the meta-analyses due to heterogeneity and risk of bias concerns. Estimated overdiagnosis with LDCT screening was 18%, however the 95% CI was 0 to 36% (risk difference (RD) 0.18, 95% CI -0.00 to 0.36; 5 trials, 28,656 participants; low-certainty evidence). Four trials compared different aspects of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using various measures. Anxiety was pooled from three trials, with participants in LDCT screening reporting lower anxiety scores than in the control group (standardised mean difference (SMD) -0.43, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.27; 3 trials, 8153 participants; low-certainty evidence). There were insufficient data to comment on the impact of LDCT screening on smoking behaviour.  AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: The current evidence supports a reduction in lung cancer-related mortality with the use of LDCT for lung cancer screening in high-risk populations (those over the age of 40 with a significant smoking exposure). However, there are limited data on harms and further trials are required to determine participant selection and optimal frequency and duration of screening, with potential for significant overdiagnosis of lung cancer. Trials are ongoing for lung cancer screening in non-smokers.

documents.title: Exhaled VOC detection in lung cancer screening: a comprehensive meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer (LC), characterized by high incidence and mortality rates, presents a significant challenge in oncology. Despite advancements in treatments, early detection remains crucial for improving patient outcomes. The accuracy of screening for LC by detecting volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in exhaled breath remains to be determined.
METHODS: Our systematic review, following PRISMA guidelines and analyzing data from 25 studies up to October 1, 2023, evaluates the effectiveness of different techniques in detecting VOCs. We registered the review protocol with PROSPERO and performed a systematic search in PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science. Reviewers screened the studies' titles/abstracts and full texts, and used QUADAS-2 tool for quality assessment. Then performed meta-analysis by adopting a bivariate model for sensitivity and specificity.
RESULTS: This study explores the potential of VOCs in exhaled breath as biomarkers for LC screening, offering a non-invasive alternative to traditional methods. In all studies, exhaled VOCs discriminated LC from controls. The meta-analysis indicates an integrated sensitivity and specificity of 85% and 86%, respectively, with an AUC of 0.93 for VOC detection. We also conducted a systematic analysis of the source of the substance with the highest frequency of occurrence in the tested compounds. Despite the promising results, variability in study quality and methodological challenges highlight the need for further research.
CONCLUSION: This review emphasizes the potential of VOC analysis as a cost-effective, non-invasive screening tool for early LC detection, which could significantly improve patient management and survival rates.
documents.conclusions: This review emphasizes the potential of VOC analysis as a cost-effective, non-invasive screening tool for early LC detection, which could significantly improve patient management and survival rates.
