Single-agent ICI (Mono IO) versus platinum-based CT – high TMB As far as ORR is concerned, the administration of single-agent IO regimens reflected a trend favoring disease debulking, albeit not statistically significant (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.90-1.54). In our analysis, this effect also turned into a clear effect in PFS (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.62-0.86) and OS (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.59-0.83), supporting the use of single-agent ICIs in the TMB-high subgroup ( Supplementary Figure S3 , available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2021.100124 ). Single-agent ICI (Mono IO) versus platinum-based CT – low TMB Even if only two cohorts could be considered when evaluating ORR in this setting, the administration of CT alone produced a greater result over single-agent IO (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.95), however with no significant benefit in OS (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.91-1.17). Interestingly, PFS pooled results underlined a statistical significance in favor of standard CT over IO regimens (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.12-1.56) in TMB-low patients ( Supplementary Figure S4 , available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2021.100124 ). Combination ICIs (Combo IO) versus platinum-based CT – high TMB Our pooled results showed clear statistically significant differences in terms of all the outcomes including ORR (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.06-2.72), PFS (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47-0.92), and OS (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.52-0.78), favoring the combination ICI strategy over standard CT in TMB-high patients ( Supplementary Figure S5 , available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2021.100124 ). Combination ICIs (Combo IO) versus platinum-based CT – low TMB As regards ORR, even if only data of the blood cohort from the MYSTIC trial could be evaluated, the administration of CT alone was more active in terms of response (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.37-0.77), however with no significant difference in OS (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.74-1.50). Intriguingly, PFS pooled results demonstrated a great benefit in favor of CT alone over the combination strategy (HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.05-2.05) in TMB-low patients ( Supplementary Figure S6 , available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2021.100124 ). Risk of bias assessment In our analysis, publication bias Egger's test was calculated for every outcome showing no statistical significance ( Supplementary Figure S7 , available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2021.100124 ). The overall quality assessment was evaluated according to the CONSORT checklist statement. We reported an average good quality of all trials. Some problems related to ‘Blinding of participants and personnel’ (performance bias) domains because studies were reported as open-label designs ( Supplementary Figure S8 , available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2021.100124 ). Discussion This meta-analysis focused the attention on the clinical utility of TMB as a predictive biomarker of the response to immunotherapy in the first-line setting of advanced non-oncogene addicted NSCLC patients treated with ICIs compared with standard CT alone. Most selected studies evaluating the potential role of TMB in such patients seemed to suggest that TMB would not be ready for prime-time yet, requiring a careful assessment for its routine use in clinical practice. 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 Accordingly, there is still the need to identify those TMB-high patients who do not respond to immune checkpoint blockade, aiming to evaluate additional genetic features associated with the anticancer immune response. 42 , 43 Furthermore, whether all the different IO agents are equally effective across the TMB spectrum in advanced-stage NSCLC patients is still unknown. 44 , 45 , 46 In this context, the lack of standardization for TMB calculation with different platforms reporting different TMB expression thresholds must be considered. 47 , 48 , 49 Of note, recent analyses in advanced NSCLC patients who received ICIs highlighted that TMB and PD-L1 expression may be uncorrelated, suggesting that they could be independent predictive biomarkers that can each contribute to the identification of patients for immune-based therapy. 50 , 51 , 52 In this scenario, we hypothesized that PD-L1 might not be the sole guiding biomarker in the first-line setting of advanced NSCLC without targetable genetic alterations and inferred that the complementary use of tissue TMB monitoring could be implemented in the clinic to improve patient selection. Since direct comparison studies will be unlikely in this setting, we compared different IO agents versus standard CT alone to identify any potential differences in efficacy outcomes within two main TMB subgroups. We encompassed publicly available results from first-line randomized phase III studies testing IO strategies, including direct randomized evidence on treatments of interest along with indirect evidence and exploratory analyses from randomized studies with platinum CT as the common comparator. Even if the trial designs slightly differed according to the different available ICI combinations, the setting and the efficacy outcomes stratified by TMB status were the same in all these studies. Overall, 35% and 65% of the patients included in this meta-analysis were TMB-high and -low, respectively. The results of this meta-analysis demonstrated that, when assigned to receive IO agents versus platinum-based CT, TMB-high patients showed a remarkable effect in ORR and a statistically significant benefit in PFS along with an unprecedented OS improvement compared with those patients featuring a low-TMB status. Conversely, in TMB-low patients, no OS benefit in favor of one treatment or another has been observed, whereas CT was more active and associated with a reduced risk of progressing disease when compared with IO agents. Focusing on the pre-planned subgroup analysis, our results confirmed that, when compared with CT alone, both single-agent and combination ICIs were associated with a statistically significant advantage in terms of PFS and OS within the TMB-high subgroup; however, as regards activity in this setting, the dual checkpoint blockade appeared to be associated with an increased response rate whereas the IO monotherapy did not reach the statistical significance in the subgroup of patients with high TMB. As far as the TMB-low subgroup is concerned, the IO strategy did not lead to any significant benefit in OS with no advantage in terms of activity and PFS, whereas in this setting, the pooled results of both ORR and PFS were intriguingly associated with a statistical significance in favor of CT over both single-agent and combination ICIs. Thus, these results demonstrated a significant improvement in efficacy outcomes in TMB-high patients undergoing first-line IO regimens as compared with CT in terms of death risk reduction and higher chances of disease debulking, especially with the administration of combination ICIs. Besides, a possible predictive role of high TMB for IO regimens could be inferred since in the TMB-low subgroup, a statistical significance in activity and progression risk reduction toward CT when compared with IO strategies has been observed, albeit not translating into significative OS differences. Accordingly, despite inconsistencies in definitions and reporting, TMB may act as a predictive biomarker in addition to PD-L1 expression for the selection of the most appropriate patients treated with ICIs. Of note, the greater magnitude of benefit in the TMB-high subgroup appeared to come from two trials (namely, KEYNOTE-042 and CheckMate-227), thus reflecting a higher heterogeneity value in the TMB-low subgroup, although the significant differences in effect size direction affecting the included studies must be considered. These results altogether suggest that TMB would strongly complement PD-L1 expression assessment and may eventually help physicians rule in the most personalized therapeutic approach based on single-agent or combination ICIs in the first-line management of advanced non-oncogene-addicted NSCLC. However, there is a need for further prospective studies using tissue and blood TMB to investigate the prediction accuracy of ICI response and the concordance across testing platforms along with sample quality control and appropriate data interpretation to reliably implement TMB as a viable biomarker in clinical practice. Limitations The present study considered the latest NSCLC results to investigate different performances between first-line IO agents and CT among TMB-selected populations. 53 Nevertheless, this study had several limitations. First, these results should always be interpreted with caution since meta-analysis is not carried out at the individual-patient level. Secondly, a caveat when interpreting results from this study is the variability of techniques that were used in individual trials for measuring TMB expression levels; in our meta-analysis, this was of no consequence for the overall analysis, but the use of different reporting detection methods and cut-off points would represent an important limitation since the subgroup breakdowns reported in each study were based on differently approved techniques and different gene panel platforms; namely, even across cohorts of the same trial, discordant cut-offs according to tissue or blood sample seemed to significantly affect the reproducibility of the threshold; moreover, other technical issues such as differing turnaround or sample storage time could finally affect TMB values. 54 Thirdly, the lack of prospective stratification by TMB status in the included RCTs should be considered; withal, mostly owing to the quantity and quality of the available sample, TMB data were not available for all the patients evaluated with differing percentages of TMB-evaluable patients among studies. Furthermore, given that a systematic evaluation of PD-L1 expression levels could not be carried out among the TMB-selected patients, our results should be prospectively confirmed by future RCTs evaluating the efficacy of combined detection of TMB and PD-L1 expression for further implementation of TMB in the clinical practice. Finally, despite the utility of such an approach in selecting patients for immune-based treatments, a cost-effectiveness analysis is eventually needed in the light of the high cost of TMB detection. Conclusions This meta-analysis provided evidence regards the OS benefit in favor of IO agents over CT alone in TMB-selected patients, highlighting the limited utility of CT alone in the TMB-high subgroup. Strikingly, the pooled results of both ORR and PFS in the TMB-low subgroup seemed to favor CT over IO strategies, thus suggesting that high TMB could be predictive for ICI efficacy in the first-line setting. In summary, although more prospective data are warranted, we postulated the hypothesis that monitoring TMB, in addition to the existing PD-L1 expression level, could represent the preferable option for future clinical research in the first-line management of advanced non-oncogene-addicted NSCLC patients. documents.title: Artificial intelligence for lung cancer: a systematic review of head‑to‑head CT, FDG PET/CT, and multimodal models across screening, staging, and prognosis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown increasing potential in lung cancer imaging, particularly in detection, staging, prognosis, and recurrence prediction. However, there is limited synthesis of head-to-head comparative evidence between CT, FDG PET/CT, and multimodal fusion models within the same cohorts.
OBJECTIVES: To systematically review and critically appraise studies that directly compared CT-only, FDG PET/CT-only, and combined multimodal models in lung cancer, with emphasis on clinical setting, fusion strategy, validation design, and clinical utility.
METHODS: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language human studies published between January 1, 2019, and September 8, 2025. Eligible studies reported same-cohort, head-to-head comparisons of CT, PET/CT, or multimodal models for lung cancer screening, staging, or prognosis. Risk of bias was assessed using PROBAST for prediction model studies and SANRA for narrative reviews. Data were extracted in duplicate and synthesized narratively, with meta-analysis performed where ≥ 3 studies were sufficiently homogeneous.
RESULTS: From 2,417 records (PubMed 845, Scopus 920, IEEE Xplore 452, Google Scholar/manual 200), 31 studies met inclusion criteria (20 primary modeling studies, 11 reviews). In screening cohorts, low-dose CT deep-learning models consistently outperformed other modalities, with modest incremental value from clinical covariates. For nodal staging, integrated PET/CT radiomics-clinical models showed superior discrimination, calibration, and net-benefit compared with unimodal approaches. In prognostic and recurrence settings, fused PET/CT models outperformed CT- or PET-only models across institutions, with further improvement from clinical variables. Radiogenomics and pathology integration provided added value but were limited by small samples and lack of external validation.
CONCLUSIONS: Comparative evidence demonstrates that modality performance is context-dependent: CT dominates in screening, PET/CT fusion excels in staging and prognosis, and multimodal integration with clinical or biomarker data enhances discrimination and utility. Standardization, harmonization, and rigorous external validation remain critical for generalizability.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.
documents.conclusions: Comparative evidence demonstrates that modality performance is context-dependent: CT dominates in screening, PET/CT fusion excels in staging and prognosis, and multimodal integration with clinical or biomarker data enhances discrimination and utility. Standardization, harmonization, and rigorous external validation remain critical for generalizability.

Keywords Lung neoplasms Tomography, X-Ray computed Positron-emission tomography and computed tomography Radiomics Artificial intelligence pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2026 Introduction Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, and imaging—particularly low‑dose chest CT for screening and FDG PET/CT for staging and response—anchors radiologists’ workflows across the care continuum [ 1 , 2 ]. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly in lung cancer imaging, targeting detection, nodule characterization, staging, prognosis, and biomarker inference with growing relevance for radiology practice [ 2 , 3 ]. Low‑dose CT is the backbone of screening, where modern deep‑learning and radiomics models demonstrate strong performance, with additional gains when clinical data are incorporated [ 2 , 4 , 5 ]. FDG PET/CT is integral to mediastinal staging and treatment planning, and AI/radiomics approaches aim to exploit complementary metabolic and morphologic information [ 1 , 3 ]. Across clinical settings, recent comparative evaluations indicate there is no universal best model: single‑timepoint CT AI tends to excel in screening cohorts, whereas longitudinal imaging and multimodal models often perform better for incidentally detected nodules [ 6 , 7 ]. Head‑to‑head, same‑cohort studies show that PET/CT fusion generally outperforms PET‑only or CT‑only for prognostic modeling, with clinical variables providing incremental value [ 8 – 10 ]. For thoracic lymph node metastasis in early invasive adenocarcinoma, an integrated PET/CT radiomics–clinical model outperformed individual radiomics or clinical models and demonstrated favorable calibration and decision‑curve utility [ 11 ]. When PET/CT is unavailable, CT‑based deep‑learning features can yield strong postoperative progression prediction, and adding clinicopathologic variables confers modest but meaningful net‑benefit gains [ 12 ]. In screening‑oriented risk prediction, multimodal integration of CT with clinical data and blood biomarkers—implemented with explicit missing‑modality handling—improves discrimination while retaining patients with incomplete data [ 13 , 14 ]. Radiogenomics studies fusing CT features with tumor gene expression suggest added signal for recurrence and survival prediction, though sample sizes are small and external validations are limited [ 15 – 17 ]. However, heterogeneity in acquisition and reconstruction, small and imbalanced cohorts, and limited cross‑site validation frequently impair generalizability, with multicenter delta‑PET/CT work underscoring reproducibility challenges [ 3 , 18 , 19 ]. Radiologists currently lack use‑case–anchored, availability‑aware guidance distilled from head‑to‑head, same‑cohort comparisons across screening, staging, and prognosis to inform modality and fusion choices [ 6 , 8 , 11 ]. Inconsistent cohorts, protocols, and metrics—together with limited external validation and calibration—undermine generalizability and hinder clinical adoption of AI models [ 3 , 12 , 18 ]. Most multimodal studies do not model missing modalities at train/test, limiting utility when clinical, biomarker, or genomics data are sporadically available in real‑world radiology [ 13 , 14 , 16 ]. Accordingly, best‑practice recommendations emphasize IBSI‑compliant pipelines, PET/CT harmonization (e.g., reconstruction and SUV standardization), rigorous calibration, and external or cross‑site validation using task‑appropriate metrics [ 3 , 19 ]. Existing reviews are largely narrative and broad, providing limited synthesis of use‑case–anchored, head‑to‑head evidence that radiologists can apply directly to modality selection and fusion strategy [ 2 , 3 , 20 ]. Across the recent literature, a consistent pattern emerges in which multimodal approaches outperform unimodal baselines. FDG PET/CT generally improves upon PET or CT alone for staging and prognosis, CT-based deep-learning models outperform conventional CT assessment in screening and risk stratification, and integrated radiomics–clinical or imaging–clinical models consistently exceed the performance of imaging-only or clinical-only models [ 3 , 19 , 21 ]. These hierarchical gains suggest that complementary information across modalities and data types is biologically meaningful rather than redundant [ 13 , 14 , 16 , 22 ]. Despite this apparent progress, most studies stop short of translating performance improvements into practical, use-case–specific guidance for radiologists. Comparative results are often reported without explicit consideration of modality availability, clinical workflow, calibration, or net clinical benefit, and many multimodal studies are limited by small single-center cohorts, heterogeneous acquisition protocols, incomplete external validation, and optimistic internal testing. As a result, radiologists are frequently left without clear evidence-based direction regarding when CT alone is sufficient, when PET/CT meaningfully alters decision-making, and when additional multimodal fusion is justified in routine practice. This systematic review aims to critically appraise and synthesize head‑to‑head comparisons of CT, FDG PET/CT, and multimodal AI models across screening, nodal staging, and prognosis in lung cancer, emphasizing clinical setting, fusion design, handling of missing modalities, harmonization, validation strategy, and clinically meaningful metrics to inform radiology practice. Methods Reporting framework and protocol We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) [ 23 ] and the PRISMA-S [ 24 ] extension for reporting literature searches; an a priori protocol specifying the research questions, eligibility criteria, and analysis plan was developed before screening commenced. We adhered to PRISMA flow-diagram conventions for documenting the study selection process and prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses in the protocol. We targeted literature published from January 1, 2019, through September 8, 2025, to align with the maturation of contemporary comparative imaging studies in lung cancer. Research questions In head-to-head, same-cohort evaluations, how do CT-only models compare with FDG PET/CT-only and combined CT + FDG PET/CT models for screening, nodal staging, and prognosis/recurrence tasks in lung cancer? When multiple modalities are available, which fusion strategies (e.g., feature-level, image-level, intermediate, or late fusion) are associated with superior discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility within each clinical setting? How does performance vary by clinical context (screening-detected nodules, incidentally detected nodules, and biopsy-selected cohorts), and are there consistent “winners” within each use case? What is the incremental value of adding clinical variables, blood biomarkers, histopathology, or genomics to imaging, and how do studies handle missingness of these non-imaging modalities? To what extent do studies implement external, temporal, or cross-site validation, and how does validation design affect reported performance and generalizability? How frequently are harmonization and standardization practices (e.g., reconstruction/SUV standardization for PET/CT, IBSI-compliant feature extraction for CT radiomics) applied, and do they modify effect estimates? Are appropriate task-specific metrics (e.g., AUROC/AUPRC for classification, c-index/IBS for time-to-event outcomes) and clinical utility analyses (calibration, decision-curve analysis) consistently reported? What are the predominant risks of bias in comparative modality studies, and how do these risks influence the strength of evidence and conclusions? Eligibility criteria We included original human studies in adults with lung cancer or pulmonary nodules that performed explicit, head-to-head comparisons of imaging modalities within the same cohort and split structure, specifically contrasting CT-only versus FDG PET/CT-only versus combined CT + FDG PET/CT, or contrasting single-modality versus multimodal models where imaging was a required component. Eligible tasks encompassed screening/nodule risk stratification, nodal metastasis/staging proxies, and prognosis/recurrence/survival. Studies needed to report discriminative performance with appropriate metrics for the task and provide enough methodological detail to appraise risk of bias and study quality. We accepted peer-reviewed journal articles and full-length peer-reviewed conference proceedings with sufficient methods and results. We restricted to English-language publications between January 1, 2019 and September 8, 2025. We excluded studies without same-cohort head-to-head modality comparisons; papers focused on physics, acquisition-only, or segmentation-only without clinical task evaluation; case reports, small case series (< 20 patients) lacking comparative analyses; pediatric or animal studies; editorials, letters, commentaries, and narrative reviews (retained only for background); studies mixing cohorts across distinct clinical indications or time periods in ways that confound modality comparisons without matched subsets; and studies with inadequate reporting precluding risk-of-bias assessment or data extraction. When multiple papers reported overlapping cohorts, we prioritized the most comprehensive and methodologically robust report. Information sources and search strategy A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore from database inception to September 8, 2025, limited to the 2019–2025 publication window and English language. To mitigate publication bias and capture in-press or early-access items, we also performed a complementary manual search in Google Scholar, reviewing the first 200 results per key query and hand-screening reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH) and free-text terms covering lung cancer, computed tomography, FDG PET/CT, modality comparison, and multimodal fusion. Queries were iteratively refined with an information specialist to balance sensitivity and precision and were adapted to database-specific syntax and fields. Exact database queries and limits are provided Table 1 . Table 1 Search strategy and database queries Database Time span and limits Query (as executed) Notes PubMed/ MEDLINE 2019/01/01–2025/09/08; English; Humans (“Lung Neoplasms“[Mesh] OR “lung cancer“[tiab] OR NSCLC[tiab] OR “non-small cell lung“[tiab]) AND ((“Tomography, X-Ray Computed“[Mesh] OR CT[tiab] OR “computed tomography“[tiab] OR “low-dose CT“[tiab] OR LDCT[tiab]) OR (“Positron-Emission Tomography and Computed Tomography“[Mesh] OR PET[tiab] OR PET/CT[tiab] OR FDG[tiab] OR “positron emission“[tiab])) AND (“Artificial Intelligence“[Mesh] OR “Machine Learning“[Mesh] OR “Deep Learning“[tiab] OR radiomics[tiab] OR “radiogenomics“[tiab]) AND (screening[tiab] OR staging[tiab] OR prognosis[tiab] OR survival[tiab] OR recurrence[tiab]) Filters applied post-query (dates, English, humans). IEEE Xplore 2019–2025; English (((“lung cancer” OR NSCLC OR “non-small cell lung”) AND (CT OR “computed tomography” OR LDCT) AND (“PET/CT” OR PET OR FDG)) AND (comparison OR “head to head” OR multimodal OR fusion OR ablation)) Content types: Journals, Conferences, Early Access; fielded search across metadata and full text. Google Scholar (manual) 2019–2025; English “lung cancer” AND (CT OR “computed tomography” OR LDCT) AND (PET/CT OR PET OR FDG) AND (comparison OR “head to head” OR multimodal OR fusion) AND (screening OR staging OR prognosis OR survival OR recurrence) Screened first 200 hits per query; deduplicated against database exports; hand-searched references of key included articles. Study selection Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against eligibility criteria using a web-based screening platform. Records deemed potentially eligible by either reviewer proceeded to full-text review. The same reviewers then independently assessed full texts for inclusion; disagreements at either stage were resolved by consensus or adjudication by a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion at full-text were documented verbatim and mapped to predefined categories (e.g., no same-cohort comparison, wrong population, inadequate reporting). The PRISMA flow diagram summarizes the number of records at each stage, duplicate removals, full-text articles assessed, exclusions with reasons, and final included studies. Risk of bias and study quality assessment We assessed study quality using two design-appropriate instruments. For primary prediction-model studies (diagnostic or prognostic), we applied the Prediction Model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) [ 25 ] to appraise risk of bias across its four domains—participants, predictors, outcome, and analysis—and recorded applicability concerns separately. For narrative (non-systematic) reviews, we used the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) [ 26 ] to rate six items (justification of importance, stated aims, literature search, referencing, scientific reasoning, and presentation) on the standard 0–2 scale. All assessments were performed through a structured quality review process with multiple reviewers working independently using standardized forms; discrepancies were resolved by discussion and, when needed, adjudication by a senior reviewer. Given the heterogeneity of study designs and reporting quality, these tools were applied conservatively to allow transparent, study-by-study identification of bias domains rather than relying on aggregate quality scores. Data extraction and synthesis Data were extracted in duplicate using a piloted, standardized form. We captured study identifiers, setting and design, cohort characteristics (sample size, centers, geography, enrollment years, inclusion/exclusion criteria), clinical context (screening-detected, incidental, biopsy-selected), imaging modalities and acquisition details (CT slice thickness, kernel, contrast timing; PET reconstruction, SUV normalization, timing), region of interest definitions and segmentation procedures (manual/auto; interobserver assessment), reference standards, task definition and label time horizons, comparator arms and fusion strategies, handling of missing modalities, dataset partitioning (internal splits, cross-validation, external/temporal/geographic validation), performance metrics with uncertainty (e.g., AUROC/AUPRC, sensitivity/specificity at prespecified thresholds, c-index/IBS, calibration slope/intercept, Brier score), clinical utility analyses (decision-curve analysis, net benefit), harmonization/standardization steps (e.g., IBSI compliance, ComBat/EARL constraints), and statistical tests for comparative performance (e.g., DeLong tests, log-rank tests, bootstrap CIs). When multiple analyses were reported, we prioritized prespecified primary outcomes, external validation results, and patient-level metrics. Additionally, we extracted reported details on hyperparameter selection and model-tuning strategies (e.g., grid/random search, cross-validation splits, regularization methods) for AI/radiomics models. Hyperparameter tuning practices were inconsistently documented across studies; among those that provided details, common approaches included the use of nested cross-validation for radiomics-based models and adaptive learning rates with early stopping for deep-learning architectures. This variability in tuning rigor and reporting may influence performance comparisons and should be considered when interpreting reported superiority across modalities. Given the substantial clinical, methodological, and reporting heterogeneity across studies—including differences in clinical setting, imaging protocols, AI architectures, outcome definitions, and validation designs—a quantitative meta-analysis was not appropriate. Therefore, no statistical pooling of effect estimates was performed. Instead, we conducted a structured narrative synthesis, organizing findings by clinical task (screening, nodal staging, prognosis/recurrence) and emphasizing head-to-head, same-cohort comparisons. Comparative performance was interpreted qualitatively based on direction and consistency of effects, reported confidence intervals, validation design, and risk-of-bias considerations, rather than pooled summary estimates. Analytical synthesis focused on cross-study comparison to identify methodological and clinical drivers of reported performance (e.g., imaging modality, fusion strategy, and validation design), rather than descriptive listing of results, given the heterogeneity of the evidence base. Results Study selection process The systematic search across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by a manual search of Google Scholar and reference lists, yielded a total of 2,417 records (Fig. 1 ). After removing 488 duplicates, 1,929 unique records underwent title and abstract screening against the eligibility criteria. During the title and abstract screening phase, 1,832 records were excluded. The primary reasons for exclusion at this stage were: the study did not involve artificial intelligence (AI) or radiomics ( n = 702); the study was not focused on lung cancer or pulmonary nodules ( n = 455); the paper was a review, editorial, or commentary without original data ( n = 347); the study did not perform a head-to-head comparison of imaging modalities (e.g., CT vs. PET/CT) ( n = 208); or the study was conducted on animals, in pediatric populations, or was a case report/small series ( n = 120). The remaining 97 articles were selected for full-text review. Upon detailed assessment, 66 articles were excluded for the following reasons: No same-cohort head-to-head comparison of the specified modalities (CT, PET/CT, multimodal) ( n = 28). Inadequate reporting of methodology or results, precluding risk-of-bias assessment or data extraction ( n = 15). Wrong study design (e.g., protocol paper, narrative review retained only for background) ( n = 11). Focus on segmentation, acquisition, or physics without clinical task evaluation ( n = 7). Overlapping cohort with a more comprehensive or recent publication that was already included ( n = 5). This process resulted in the final inclusion of 31 articles for data extraction and synthesis. Bars are colored by overall quality: High (green), Moderate (orange), Low (red) Data extraction and study characteristics We extracted data in duplicate with a piloted, standardized form across 31 articles. Twenty are primary modeling studies spanning screening/nodule risk, nodal staging, prognosis/recurrence, and radiogenomics/pathomics [ 6 – 18 , 27 – 33 ]; eleven are narrative or focused reviews synthesizing modality–task evidence rather than presenting new cohorts [ 1 – 4 , 19 , 20 , 34 – 38 ]. Among primaries, external or cross‑site validation appeared in a minority [ 8 , 12 – 14 ], plus cross‑institution train/test swaps in [ 8 , 10 ]; explicit decision‑curve or net‑benefit analyses were reported in few [ 11 , 12 ]. Only one study explicitly modeled missing modalities at train/test [ 13 ]. PET/CT works most often reported head‑to‑head unimodal vs. fused comparisons [ 8 – 11 , 31 ]; CT‑only studies frequently fused clinical variables with modest incremental gains [ 12 , 14 , 28 – 30 , 33 ]. Imaging acquisition/standardization details (slice thickness, kernels; PET reconstruction/SUV normalization) and interobserver segmentation assessments were variably incomplete, with more rigor in PET/CT radiomics papers (e.g., IBSI compatibility and ICC filtering in [ 11 ] and multicenter caveats highlighted in delta‑radiomics [ 18 ]. A full report of all extracted items is provided in Supplementary File 2 . Head-to-head performance: CT vs. FDG PET/CT vs. multimodal models In the screening setting, the head-to-head, same-cohort evaluations available in this set contrast CT-only models against clinical-only and CT+clinical models; there are no screening cohorts in which FDG PET/CT-only or CT + FDG PET/CT models were evaluated alongside CT in a controlled, within-cohort fashion. Across large screening datasets, single–time-point LDCT deep-learning models form the strongest unimodal baseline, with consistent but generally modest incremental gains when tabular clinical data elements are fused; these conclusions were shown within NLST/VLSP for CT versus CT+clinical and reproduced in broader multi-cohort comparisons focused on screening use cases. PET/CT is not part of lung cancer screening workflows and thus has not been studied head-to-head against LDCT in these screening cohorts. Consequently, for screening tasks the evidence base supports CT-centric modeling (optionally with clinical covariates) and provides no within-cohort evidence that PET/CT-only or CT + PET/CT would outperform CT alone [ 1 , 2 , 4 , 6 , 7 , 14 , 33 ]. For preoperative thoracic nodal metastasis prediction, a same-cohort, multi‑arm study directly compared CT radiomics, PET radiomics, combined PET/CT radiomics, a clinical model, and an integrated PET/CT radiomics–clinical model. Within that single cohort and using identical splits, both PET radiomics and CT radiomics were inferior to PET/CT radiomics, and the integrated PET/CT radiomics–clinical model was superior to all unimodal models, achieving the highest discrimination with appropriate calibration and decision‑curve benefit in the independent test partition (AUC ~ 0.94). These results align with the established clinical role of FDG PET/CT for mediastinal staging and indicate that, in a head‑to‑head setting, CT-only underperforms PET/CT-only, and the fusion of CT and PET (especially when combined with key clinical variables) performs best for nodal staging [ 1 , 11 ]. For overall survival and postoperative recurrence risk, multiple head‑to‑head, same‑cohort evaluations show a consistent hierarchy. In two‑institution studies that trained on one site and tested on the other using the same patient cohorts and endpoints, PET/CT radiomics constructed by either feature‑level or image‑level fusion outperformed PET-only and CT-only models; the gains held under cross‑institution evaluation, and adding clinical covariates further improved performance. Similarly, in a postoperative cohort analyzed with identical splits, models built on clinical + PET/CT features surpassed clinical + CT and clinical + PET variants, with fused PET/CT features providing the strongest recurrence prediction. A separate surgical series integrating CT tumor/peritumoral radiomics with PET metrics and clinical/qualitative variables showed improved risk stratification relative to unimodal baselines within the same cohort, again pointing to added value from combining PET and CT rather than relying on CT alone. Together, these within‑cohort comparisons indicate that for prognostic/recurrence tasks CT-only models are generally weaker than PET/CT-only models, and combined CT + PET/CT models are superior to either modality alone [ 8 – 10 , 31 ]. Importantly, the strength of evidence addressing RQ1 was not uniform across clinical contexts. Same-cohort, head-to-head comparisons were robust and internally consistent for nodal staging and for prognosis-related outcomes, enabling clear modality hierarchies to be established. In contrast, for screening applications, no eligible studies incorporated FDG PET/CT within the same cohort, precluding direct comparison against CT-only or combined PET/CT–CT strategies. As such, conclusions for screening are necessarily constrained to CT-centered models, and the absence of PET/CT evidence should be interpreted as an evidence gap rather than evidence of inferiority. Comparison of fusion strategies Within screening cohorts built around low-dose, non-contrast CT, the only same-cohort multimodal comparisons in this set fuse CT with tabular information rather than PET. In NLST/VLSP, an intermediate “co-learning” strategy that jointly learns from whole-scan CT and clinical data elements achieved higher discrimination than either CT-only or clinical-only baselines, demonstrating that integrated feature learning from CT plus clinical covariates is advantageous when both are present; calibration and decision-curve analyses were not the focus in this work, but the discrimination gains reproduced internally and on a geographic external test set, indicating robustness of the intermediate fusion approach in the screening context [ 14 ]. A second screening study on NLST contrasted several fusion choices and found that concatenating learned CT features with clinical variables and training a unified classifier (an intermediate/feature-level fusion) outperformed score-level late fusion, again pointing to joint representation learning as the better strategy for discrimination when CT and clinical data are available; calibration and clinical-utility analyses were not reported there [ 33 ]. A related multimodal risk model that added blood biomarkers to CT and clinical data employed a multi-path network with modality-specific encoders and an attention-based aggregation (effectively an intermediate fusion with explicit missing-modality handling); this design significantly improved discrimination over single-modality models and preserved performance when modalities were absent at inference, a property that is practically important in screening programs where ancillary data are sporadic, although calibration and decision-curve metrics were not emphasized [ 13 ]. Taken together, the head-to-head evidence in screening supports intermediate fusion of CT with tabular data as the most reliable route to better discrimination, with explicit missingness-aware designs further strengthening performance and generalizability beyond CT alone; PET-based fusion is not represented in same-cohort screening evaluations in this corpus [ 6 , 7 , 13 , 14 , 33 ]. For preoperative thoracic lymph-node metastasis, a single-center but carefully controlled study directly compared multiple fusion strategies within the same cohort and splits: PET-only radiomics, CT-only radiomics, PET/CT radiomics fused at the feature level, a clinical-only model, and an integrated PET/CT radiomics–clinical model. Feature-level fusion of PET and CT already improved discrimination over either modality alone, and adding clinical variables in the same feature-level framework yielded the best overall performance with high test AUC and favorable calibration; importantly, the authors complemented ROC analyses with decision-curve evaluation, showing superior net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds for the integrated PET/CT+clinical model. In this nodal-staging setting—where PET and CT are spatially co-registered and biologically complementary—feature-level fusion, further augmented with clinical covariates, is therefore the strategy with the strongest evidence for superior discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility within a head-to-head design [ 11 ]. This conclusion is consistent with the established staging role of PET/CT in lung cancer, though the comparative fusion analysis itself rests on the single but internally validated study above [ 1 ]. Across survival and recurrence tasks, the most comprehensive same-cohort comparisons pit PET-only, CT-only, and fused PET/CT models with and without clinical variables, and they evaluate both feature-level and image-level fusion. In a two-institution program that swapped training and testing across sites, multi-level PET/CT fusion—either by concatenating modality-specific radiomic features (feature-level) or by constructing a fused image via wavelet-based PET/CT blending prior to feature extraction (image-level)—consistently outperformed single-modality models for overall survival, with the fusion gains persisting under cross-site evaluation; incorporating clinical covariates on top of the fused imaging further improved concordance, underscoring the value of adding complementary non-imaging signals once PET and CT have been integrated [ 8 , 10 ]. In a postoperative recurrence cohort, an image-level guided-filter fusion of PET and CT combined with clinical variables produced the best recurrence prediction in head-to-head analyses against clinical-only, clinical + CT, and clinical + PET variants, supporting the conclusion that when PET/CT is available, image-level fusion followed by modeling can yield superior discrimination relative to single-modality or simpler combinations; calibration metrics were not detailed, but improvements reached statistical significance in comparative tests within the same splits [ 9 ]. A separate surgical series that integrated PET- and CT-derived features from tumor and peri-tumoral regions with qualitative CT findings and clinical variables using a feature-level survival ensemble also achieved better risk stratification than stage-only or unimodal models in within-cohort evaluations, reinforcing that comprehensive feature-level fusion across PET, CT, and clinical/qualitative data enhances prognostic separation; while formal calibration curves were not the focus, performance improvements were reflected in concordance and Kaplan–Meier separation on the held-out test set [ 30 , 31 ]. For settings where PET is not available, combining deep CT representations with clinicopathologic variables using a straightforward feature/late-fusion classifier yielded small but statistically significant discrimination gains and, crucially, better decision-curve net benefit than either source alone, indicating improved clinical utility even when imaging dominates the signal; this study also included external temporal/geographic validation, strengthening the case for this fusion choice in CT-only workflows [ 12 ]. Finally, when imaging is fused with high-dimensional omics rather than PET, the radiogenomics studies in this set show that late fusion of modality-specific risk scores in regularized Cox models or nomograms can match or exceed more elaborate non-linear intermediate fusion under small-sample constraints, improving discrimination without overfitting; however, calibration and decision-curve analyses were seldom reported, and external validation was limited, so these gains should be treated as provisional with respect to clinical utility [ 15 , 16 ]. In sum, the fusion strategy that is associated with the best performance depends on the alignment and heterogeneity of the modalities and on the clinical setting. In screening, intermediate co-learning of CT with tabular data—and designs explicitly tolerant to missing inputs—has the clearest within-cohort evidence for improving discrimination over either source alone [ 13 , 14 , 33 ]. In nodal staging with paired FDG PET/CT, feature-level PET + CT fusion augmented by clinical variables stands out as the only approach in this corpus to demonstrate, in the same cohort, simultaneous gains in discrimination together with favorable calibration and superior decision-curve net benefit, supporting its clinical utility for this task [ 11 ]. In prognosis and recurrence, both image-level and feature-level PET/CT fusion outperform unimodal imaging consistently across institutions, with further incremental benefit from adding clinical covariates; where PET is unavailable, simple feature/late fusion of CT with clinicopathologic variables can still improve discrimination and net benefit, and late-fusion Cox approaches are a pragmatic choice when integrating CT with genomics under sample-size limitations [ 8 – 10 , 12 , 15 , 16 , 31 ]. Taken together, the comparative evidence addressing RQ2 remains necessarily task-specific rather than universal. In screening and risk stratification contexts, intermediate or feature-level fusion strategies—particularly those integrating CT with clinical or biomarker data—consistently outperformed unimodal approaches and late score-level fusion, while demonstrating favorable calibration and external generalizability. In contrast, PET/CT fusion strategy comparisons are largely confined to nodal staging and selected prognostic settings, where feature-level fusion of PET and CT, further augmented by clinical variables, yielded the most robust discrimination and clinical utility. Direct, head-to-head comparisons between image-level, feature-level, and intermediate fusion remain limited to a small number of isolated studies, precluding a quantitative or task-agnostic ranking of fusion strategies. Performance variation by clinical context Across screening-detected nodules, incidentally detected nodules, and biopsy-selected cohorts, head-to-head multi-cohort evaluations show that the best-performing modality and model class depend on the use case, with no single approach consistently superior across all contexts [ 6 , 7 ]. In screening-detected nodules from low-dose CT programs, single-timepoint CT deep-learning models provided the strongest discrimination within screening cohorts, and adding clinical risk factors yielded modest but reproducible improvements when such data were available [ 6 , 7 , 14 , 33 ]. These screening observations align with low-dose CT being the established screening modality and PET/CT not being part of screening workflows, so same-cohort PET/CT comparisons are not represented in these datasets [ 2 , 4 , 6 ]. For incidentally detected nodules, performance improved when models incorporated longitudinal imaging or fused imaging with clinical and biomarker information, whereas single-timepoint CT models optimized for screening underperformed in this setting [ 6 , 7 , 13 ]. Within these incidental-use cohorts, integrating consecutive CT examinations and relevant clinical features achieved higher discrimination than clinical-only baselines and generalized better than screening-trained single-scan models [ 7 , 14 ]. In biopsy-selected cohorts enriched for highly suspicious lesions, all evaluated approaches—including clinical risk scores, CT-only AI, longitudinal imaging, and multimodal models—showed degraded performance with no clearly superior method [ 6 , 7 ]. Consequently, there are no consistent “winners” across contexts: CT-centric models are most effective in pure screening cohorts, multimodal and longitudinal strategies offer advantages for incidentally detected nodules, and no approach clearly dominates in biopsy-selected cohorts where overall performance is uniformly lower [ 6 , 7 , 13 , 14 ]. Furthermore, applying models outside their development context led to notable performance drops, reinforcing that modality and fusion choices must be tailored to the specific clinical use case [ 6 , 7 ]. Collectively, the evidence addressing RQ3 indicates that model performance is strongly conditioned by clinical context, and that no single modality or modeling strategy consistently dominates across screening-detected, incidental, and biopsy-selected cohorts. Screening-detected populations favor CT-centered models augmented by clinical variables, whereas nodal staging and postoperative prognostic settings consistently favor PET/CT-based multimodal fusion with clinical data. Evidence from multi-cohort reimplementation further demonstrates that model rankings shift substantially across screening, incidental, and biopsy-enriched cohorts, reflecting spectrum effects and differences in disease prevalence. While these findings establish context dependency as a central principle, evidence for incidental and biopsy-selected nodules remains comparatively sparse and heterogeneous, limiting systematic conclusions for these cohorts. Incremental value of non-imaging modalities and handling of missing data Adding clinical variables to imaging improves discrimination in multiple lung cancer settings, with consistent gains in screening when whole‑scan LDCT is co‑learned with clinical data elements in NLST and externally in VLSP, and with further advantages reported in multi‑cohort comparisons that emphasize the benefit of combining imaging with clinical risk factors outside pure screening [ 7 , 14 ]. In the same‑cohort nodal‑staging study, integrating clinical variables with PET/CT radiomics yielded the highest test AUC with favorable calibration and superior decision‑curve net benefit compared with PET‑only, CT‑only, and PET/CT‑only radiomics, demonstrating incremental clinical utility from adding clinical data to imaging [ 11 ]. For prognosis and postoperative progression, CT deep‑learning features already performed strongly, but adding clinicopathologic variables conferred a small yet statistically significant improvement and better decision‑curve net benefit, indicating incremental value even when imaging dominates the signal [ 12 ]. In postoperative recurrence and survival studies that fused PET and CT, adding clinical variables further improved prognostic performance over imaging‑only baselines, reinforcing that clinical covariates provide additive information when combined with fused PET/CT features [ 8 ]. Incorporating blood biomarkers alongside CT and clinical features can significantly enhance lung cancer risk prediction while maintaining robustness to sporadic availability, as a multi‑path network explicitly designed for missing modalities showed that CT+clinical+biomarker fusion outperformed any single modality and that training on incomplete cases improved discriminatory power [ 13 ]. Beyond risk prediction, a large GGN study built a multimodal deep model that merged CT with general patient data and serum tumor markers, explored different combinations, and compared against radiologists, underscoring that serum markers are actively integrated with imaging to boost invasiveness stratification within the same cohort [ 29 ]. In broader use‑case analyses of nodule cohorts, multimodal approaches that include non‑imaging signals such as biomarkers are reported to benefit incidentally detected nodules compared with single‑timepoint CT models tuned for screening, suggesting incremental value when biomarker data are present [ 7 ]. Adding histopathology through whole‑slide images contributes additional predictive signal when fused with imaging and clinical data, as a radiotherapy‑focused study that combined CT radiomics, WSI pathomics, and clinical variables found that late fusion outperformed each unimodal model and early fusion on the same patients, indicating incremental discrimination from pathology integration despite a small sample size [ 27 ]. Although this cohort was limited, the within‑cohort advantage of adding WSI to imaging aligns with the broader view that heterogeneous modalities can provide complementary information for treatment‑outcome prediction [ 27 ]. Genomics adds measurable prognostic value when fused with CT features, as a radiogenomics study using elastic‑net Cox modeling reported up to a roughly 10% absolute c‑index improvement for CT + RNA‑seq over either modality alone in the same 5‑fold cross‑validation framework [ 15 ]. A late‑fusion nomogram that combined modality‑specific risk scores from CT radiomics and gene‑expression with clinical covariates achieved higher concordance than unimodal models on the TCIA radiogenomics cohort, demonstrating incremental benefit from genomics and clinical information beyond imaging alone [ 16 ]. More recent multimodal architectures that integrate handcrafted and deep CT features with gene data via attention or adaptive fusion also improved discrimination over unimodal baselines on their internal cohorts, supporting the added value of genomics, albeit with limited details on calibration or external validation in the excerpts provided [ 17 , 32 ]. Most multimodal studies in this set assume complete availability of non‑imaging modalities at both training and inference, without explicit mechanisms for missing‑modality robustness, whereas the missingness‑aware design in the multi‑path biomarker study is a notable exception [ 11 – 15 , 31 , 33 ]. In screening, CT+clinical co‑learning improved performance but did not detail missing‑modality inference, consistent with many fusion works that require all inputs, while the biomarker‑aware network demonstrated end‑to‑end training and inference when modalities were absent, highlighting divergent handling of missingness across studies [ 13 , 14 ]. In nodal staging and recurrence/survival cohorts, integrated PET/CT+clinical models and PET/CT fusion pipelines reported superior discrimination and net benefit but did not describe strategies for test‑time absence of clinical or other non‑imaging data, further emphasizing that explicit missingness handling remains uncommon outside specialized designs [ 8 , 9 , 11 , 31 ]. Calibration and clinical‑utility reporting accompany some multimodal gains but are uneven across modalities, as the PET/CT‑clinical nodal model provided calibration and decision‑curve analyses that favored the fused approach, whereas screening co‑learning and several radiogenomics papers primarily reported discrimination metrics without detailed calibration or net‑benefit evaluations [ 11 , 14 – 17 ] (Table 2 ). Overall, the evidence addressing RQ4 indicates a consistent and reproducible incremental benefit of incorporating clinical variables alongside imaging across screening, nodal staging, and prognostic contexts. In contrast, the added value of blood biomarkers, pathology-derived features, and genomic data is supported by only a small number of studies, often limited to single-center cohorts without external validation, precluding quantitative synthesis or task-independent conclusions. Radiogenomic approaches, while promising, remain exploratory and insufficiently validated for clinical translation. With respect to missing non-imaging modalities, explicit modeling of modality absence during training and inference was observed in only one study, whereas most investigations relied implicitly on complete-case analysis or excluded patients with missing data, limiting real-world applicability. Impact of validation design on generalizability Across the included studies, validation practices range from multi-institution external testing to single-center internal cross-validation, with many modality-fusion reports relying solely on internal splits [ 8 , 11 , 14 – 16 , 27 , 33 ]. Large comparative efforts explicitly evaluate models across distinct cohorts and clinical settings, whereas numerous single-institution works report performance without geographic or temporal hold-outs that would test transportability [ 6 , 7 , 11 , 15 , 27 , 30 , 31 , 33 ]. Methodological reviews consistently emphasize that absent external and prospective validation constrains generalizability and clinical translation of lung cancer AI models [ 1 , 3 , 19 , 20 , 34 , 36 , 38 ]. In screening, a CT–clinical co-learning model developed with five-fold internal validation on NLST and tested on an external Vanderbilt cohort retained its superiority to unimodal baselines, demonstrating geographic generalization beyond the development dataset [ 14 ]. For overall survival modeling, PET/CT fusion approaches trained at one institution and evaluated at the other in a two-site swap repeatedly outperformed PET-only and CT-only comparators on the external site, indicating that the fusion advantage persists under cross-site validation [ 8 , 10 ]. For stage I postoperative progression, training in one hospital and external temporal/geographic validation in another showed that combining CT deep features with clinicopathologic variables provided a small but statistically significant AUC gain and improved decision-curve utility in the independent cohort [ 12 ]. A multi-cohort analysis that re-implemented diverse risk models found that performance rankings shift across screening, incidental, and biopsy-selected cohorts, underscoring that conclusions drawn in a single context may not generalize to other clinical spectrums [ 6 , 7 ]. By contrast, a high-AUC nodal-metastasis model with favorable calibration and decision-curve benefit was evaluated only with an internal train–test split at a single center, leaving its out-of-distribution performance uncertain [ 11 ]. Several prognosis and recurrence studies—including PET/CT fusion with nomograms and multimodal survival models that integrate PET, CT, and clinical features—reported improvements under single-center internal splits without external testing, which increases the risk of overoptimistic estimates [ 9 , 30 , 31 ]. Screening and radiogenomics works also frequently relied on internal cross-validation or single-cohort train–test partitions without independent temporal or geographic cohorts, limiting claims about deployment readiness [ 15 , 16 , 33 ]. A multicenter delta-PET/CT radiomics study directly demonstrated that inter-center and protocol heterogeneity can erase apparent prognostic signal, illustrating why external and cross-site validation are essential for credible generalization [ 18 ]. Temporal generalization was indirectly probed by training on the early-2000s NLST and testing on the mid‑2010s Vanderbilt cohort, where CT+clinical fusion maintained improvements, suggesting some robustness across time periods as well as sites [ 14 ]. Use‑case shifts across contemporary cohorts further showed that models tuned for screening degrade in biopsy-enriched cohorts, functioning as a stringent external validation at the level of disease spectrum and clinical workflow [ 6 , 7 ]. Reviews of PET/CT AI reiterate that protocol standardization and harmonization are prerequisites for reproducible longitudinal and temporal generalization, reinforcing the need to validate beyond internal cross-validation [ 1 , 3 , 35 ]. Overall, studies incorporating external, temporal, or cross-site validation tend to report more conservative yet credible performance, whereas single-center internal designs often produce higher metrics that do not reliably transport across settings [ 8 , 10 , 12 , 14 , 18 , 33 ]. Consequently, generalizability tracks validation design: cross-site swaps and independent cohorts support durable modality conclusions such as the consistent advantage of PET/CT fusion over single modalities for prognostic tasks, while internal-only evaluations cannot establish stability across institutions, time periods, or clinical spectrums [ 8 , 10 – 12 ]. A quantitative meta-analysis comparing performance across validation schemes was not feasible due to substantial heterogeneity in tasks, cohorts, outcome definitions, and reported metrics; nevertheless, consistent qualitative patterns across reimplementation and cross-site studies provide convergent evidence of validation-dependent performance inflation. Application and impact of harmonization and standardization practices Across the reviewed studies set, explicit harmonization and standardization practices are inconsistently applied in primary studies, with several influential reviews emphasizing their necessity and documenting uneven uptake across the literature [ 3 , 19 , 35 , 38 ]. In a same‑cohort nodal‑staging study, the authors implemented an IBSI‑compatible pipeline with µ ± 3σ normalization, 1 mm³ resampling, interobserver ICC filtering, and a structured feature‑selection procedure, thereby standardizing CT radiomics extraction and improving feature reliability, although no counterfactual without these steps was reported to quantify their effect on discrimination or calibration [ 11 ]. In multi‑institution prognostic work, cross‑site train–test swaps were performed without formal inter‑scanner radiomics harmonization (e.g., ComBat), relying instead on fixed gray‑level discretizations and consistent feature‑selection, which supports some generalization but leaves open whether feature‑level harmonization would further stabilize effect estimates [ 8 , 10 ]. A multicenter delta‑PET/CT radiomics study explicitly demonstrated that protocol heterogeneity across scanners and centers can abolish apparent prognostic signal, underscoring that the absence of harmonization can materially degrade effect estimates and external validity [ 18 ]. Reviews centered on PET/CT AI explicitly call for SUV normalization and reconstruction standardization (EARL‑like constraints) to improve reproducibility and multi‑site transport, indicating that such practices are not yet universal in published prognostic and staging pipelines [ 3 , 35 ]. Screening studies that fuse LDCT with clinical data focused on discrimination and external geographic testing rather than radiomics harmonization, reflecting that voxelwise IBSI pipelines are less central to end‑to‑end deep learning on whole scans in this context [ 14 , 33 ]. Radiogenomics studies and small multimodal outcome papers generally did not describe PET SUV harmonization or IBSI compliance in detail, which limits interpretability of cross‑site robustness and the stability of effect sizes [ 15 , 16 , 27 ]. Notably, a PET/CT AI review summarized examples where applying ComBat harmonization improved multicenter model performance, providing direct evidence that harmonization can favorably modify effect estimates in pooled settings [ 3 ] (Table 3 ). Across the 20 primary modeling studies, approximately one-third explicitly reported IBSI-compliant CT radiomics pipelines or PET/CT standardization steps (e.g., resampling, fixed discretization, SUV normalization), whereas fewer than 15% applied formal statistical harmonization techniques such as ComBat or EARL-aligned reconstruction constraints. Thus, while partial standardization is common, full cross-site harmonization remains uncommon in head-to-head comparative studies. Reporting of task-specific metrics and clinical utility analyses Appropriate task‑specific metrics are frequently, but not uniformly, reported, and clinical‑utility analyses such as calibration and decision‑curve analysis are available in only a subset of studies [ 1 , 3 ]. In screening, models using whole‑scan LDCT and clinical data reported AUROC and AUPRC internally with external geographic testing, aligning with classification‑task norms but without calibration or decision‑curve analyses in the main results [ 14 ]. Additional screening work on NLST used AUROC to compare fusion strategies and lacked clinical‑utility reporting, reflecting a focus on discrimination alone [ 33 ]. For nodal metastasis, the PET/CT radiomics–clinical model reported ROC AUCs with DeLong tests alongside calibration plots and decision‑curve analysis, providing a comprehensive assessment of discrimination and clinical utility [ 11 ]. In prognosis and recurrence, multiple studies used time‑to‑event metrics such as the c‑index to compare PET‑only, CT‑only, PET/CT fusion, and multimodal models, which is appropriate for survival endpoints [ 8 , 9 , 31 ]. However, some survival‑focused multimodal studies instead emphasized classification accuracy, F‑score, and recall rather than survival metrics, which is suboptimal for time‑to‑event outcomes and complicates comparison across studies [ 28 ]. Radiogenomics papers typically reported the c‑index and sometimes constructed nomograms, yet they seldom included calibration curves or decision‑curve analyses in the excerpts provided, limiting the assessment of clinical utility beyond discrimination [ 15 , 16 ]. A multicenter delta‑radiomics study focused on survival endpoints without demonstrating clinically actionable net benefit, illustrating that even when appropriate survival metrics are used, clinical‑utility analyses may be missing [ 18 ]. Reviews repeatedly advocate for task‑appropriate metrics and explicit calibration/utility analyses, confirming that current reporting remains inconsistent across the comparative‑modality literature [ 1 , 3 , 19 ]. Across the 20 primary modeling studies, task-appropriate discriminative metrics were reported in most investigations (approximately 80%), but comprehensive reporting that included both discrimination and clinical-utility assessment was uncommon. AUROC or AUPRC were consistently reported for screening and classification tasks, whereas time-to-event outcomes more variably employed survival-appropriate metrics such as the c-index. Only a small subset of studies (fewer than 25%) supplemented discrimination metrics with calibration assessment, and decision-curve analysis was reported in an even smaller fraction (approximately 10–15%), most notably in PET/CT-based nodal staging models. Thus, while basic performance reporting is common, full metric alignment with clinical decision-making remains the exception rather than the rule. For transparency, key examples of metric reporting practices across clinical tasks are summarized narratively in this section, while representative studies illustrating complete versus incomplete reporting are highlighted in Tables 2 , 3 and 4 . Predominant risks of bias and their influence on evidence strength The predominant risks of bias in comparative modality studies include spectrum and selection biases across clinical settings, small single‑center cohorts with limited events, acquisition and reconstruction heterogeneity without harmonization, incomplete external validation, class‑imbalance and prevalence shifts, and metric/reporting choices that do not match the clinical question, all of which weaken the strength of the evidence and the certainty of modality conclusions [ 1 , 3 , 19 , 34 , 36 ]. A multi‑cohort evaluation explicitly showed that models optimized for screening degrade on incidental and biopsy‑selected cohorts, demonstrating spectrum bias and indicating that modality and modeling conclusions are not portable across use cases without matched validation [ 6 , 7 ]. Several influential single‑center studies reporting gains from multimodal fusion or pathology integration rely on small samples and internal cross‑validation, introducing optimism and limiting generalizability of modality comparisons [ 27 , 30 , 31 ]. Multicenter work has demonstrated that scanner and protocol heterogeneity can extinguish apparent prognostic signal when not properly harmonized, signifying a high risk of technical bias that can flip effect direction or magnitude across sites [ 18 ]. Many studies lack independent geographic or temporal validation, which inflates apparent performance and undermines claims that one modality or fusion strategy is superior across settings [ 11 , 16 , 33 ]. Class‑imbalance and differing cancer prevalences across cohorts were highlighted as challenges in comparative evaluations, further complicating fair comparisons of modalities and thresholds [ 7 ]. Radiology and oncology reviews reiterate concerns about overfitting, inconsistent preprocessing, and potential information leakage in multimodal pipelines, cautioning that conclusions about modality superiority require rigorous design and transparent reporting to be credible [ 3 , 20 , 36 , 37 ]. Consequently, the aggregate strength of evidence favors conclusions derived from studies with same‑cohort head‑to‑head modality ablations, external or cross‑site validation, and harmonization, while internal‑only, small‑N, or heterogeneous‑acquisition studies provide weaker and less generalizable modality guidance [ 8 , 10 , 11 , 14 , 18 ]. Taken together, these bias patterns directly condition the strength of the comparative evidence. Conclusions supported by studies with low or moderate risk of bias and external or cross-site validation—such as the superiority of PET/CT fusion over single-modality imaging for prognostic tasks—can be regarded as relatively robust. In contrast, findings derived primarily from single-center, internally validated studies with small sample sizes, complex multimodal fusion, or inappropriate outcome metrics should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. Thus, risk of bias does not merely affect absolute performance estimates, but systematically shapes which modality comparisons can be considered reliable for clinical translation. Given the substantial heterogeneity in study design, modality combinations, and target tasks, we synthesized the reviewed evidence into a task-oriented summary (Table 4 ) highlighting the imaging and data integration strategies that consistently demonstrated superior performance for specific clinical applications. This table is intended to provide a pragmatic overview rather than prescriptive guidance, reflecting relative performance patterns observed across studies.
